title: The Problem Was Never What I’m Bad At
author: Kelly McGinnis
summary: Kelly McGinnis, a former CFO who left a large corporate role to build a small company, describes an evening at her desk when she realized she had crossed off seven tasks without thinking once. She traces three slips to the same cause: a developer handoff sent without the context that made it make sense, a product made too thorough for people who wanted the headline, and a cash number she tried not to look at. Each slip came from a strength that had earned her promotion, now running on reflex in a place with no organization beneath her. She argues that the instincts to cut before understanding, guard against every risk and push work off her desk were rewarded in a large company and fail in a four-person team. The essay is careful not to discard everything, since knowing what matters, anticipating what can go wrong, giving people the why and stepping back to see the forest remain sound. Her closing move is to put the pen down and make herself think instead of produce. The lesson for leaders is that changing scale means overruling strengths on purpose, not just fixing weaknesses.
points: Strengths that earned a promotion become liabilities when the environment changes, because they fire on reflex and feel like simply being good at the job.
A handoff without the why is a riddle, and thirty minutes of explaining the reasoning would have saved the developers from building the wrong thing.
The need to understand why people act does not shrink with team size; giving direction and context is leadership at ten thousand people and at four.
Over-thoroughness can be a protective habit, so feedback that a product is too much is easier to hear once you see it as a note on the work and not on you.
Stepping back to think is the first discipline to disappear under a long to-do list, and it is the one job nobody else on a small team can do for the leader.
quotes: Not once had I pulled back to ask where any of this was going. I had produced for hours and considered nothing.

The instincts slowing me down were not my weaknesses. I had beaten those years ago. The ones tripping me up now were my strengths, the exact skills I was promoted for, firing on reflex in a place that no longer rewards them.

Half of what mattered was still in my head, in the context I never stopped to write down. Thirty minutes explaining the why underneath the design and my developers would have built it right the first time.
People do not just do. They need to understand why. That is true at ten thousand people and it is true at four.
Thorough is how I earned my way into rooms I was not born into. I never believed I could coast on anything else, so I made the work airtight, because the work was the part I could always control.
The most capable version of my professional self would have vetoed my company before it ever existed.
None of that was ever wrong. What was wrong was running it on reflex, in a life that no longer has an organization beneath me, a budget to spend, or a downside I am allowed to avoid.
Growth used to mean overcoming my weaknesses. Now it means overruling my strengths.
